metadata.title: Claude, Investigation Query.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does Claude decide what actually happened when it picks up the investigation-query skill? Take the skill apart — one folder, one SKILL.md, a linear search routine read before Claude acts — and land the carry-out that a skill is a specification, not new judgment.

beats.narration_text: Liam, in for Bear. You'd guess a skill called investigation-query lets Claude work out what really happened. It doesn't. It hands Claude a search routine for one log. Let's take it apart.

beats.narration_text: Hear "Claude has an investigation-query skill" and it sounds like the model itself is cross-referencing witness accounts, weighing who's credible, deciding what really happened. That's the natural read. It's also wrong — and the reason it's wrong shows what a skill actually is.

Delete the skill's folder. The model itself doesn't change — same weights, same reasoning. What Claude loses isn't the power to judge witness credibility; it never had that. What it loses is one search routine. That's the whole diff.

Here's what a skill actually is. A folder with one file — SKILL.md. Investigation-query is exactly that: a single markdown file with instructions for querying an open investigation log — questions like what a given witness said — written in plain English. No code. No new judgment. Just a document Claude reads before it acts.

Claude reads that file top to bottom, then works each step in the order it's written. No branching. No shortcuts. Unless a step explicitly says branch, execution stays linear. That's a design choice — predictability over flexibility.

That makes a skill a specification, not new judgment. The payoff: the same search, every question, every time — reproducible. The trade-off: anything the file doesn't cover, Claude has no special opinion about. Consistency in exchange for scope.

So investigation-query never gave Claude the power to judge what a witness meant. What it guarantees is repetition: every time the skill runs, the same file gets read, the same log gets searched, the same questions get asked. Same routine, every time. That's the whole trick.

beats.narration_text: Which means watching Claude answer a question by pulling an exact quote out of the log proves the search ran — it doesn't prove Claude understood what actually happened. A quote lifted from its context is still a quote lifted from its context. And a query that comes up empty proves only that nothing matched the search, not that nothing's there. A case nobody logged is still a case.

A skill named investigation-query doesn't hand Claude the power to judge what happened — it hands Claude a checklist to read before it starts. Same log queried. Same search run. Everything outside those written steps is still your call to make.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into any frontier LLM — Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Pick one record I search the same way every time — a support log, a call history, a set of meeting notes. Write me a SKILL.md for it: plain language, ordered steps. Then read it back and walk me through exactly what you'll search for, before you search. Go deeper: once it drafts the SKILL.md, ask it to name every question the skill can't answer — and explain why that gap is a policy choice, not a bug.
